query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles, the element with the lowest melting point (copper) locally premelts at the nanoparticle surfaces to form a transient liquid layer that enhances atomic mobility and mediates the mixing of the higher-melting components. This surface‐driven premelting initiates a cascade effect that lowers the effective melting threshold and dictates the overall melting and re-solidification behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially, the nanoparticles are solid, near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys with a single-phase solid solution although subtle compositional fluctuations may exist at the nanoscale.
generation.intervention: Subject the nanoparticles to controlled heating across the premelting and melting regime while performing in situ imaging (e.g., cold neutron imaging or high-resolution TEM) and spatially resolved elemental analysis (e.g., EDX) to monitor surface and core composition changes.
generation.conditions: Heating should be conducted in an inert atmosphere over a temperature range spanning just below copper’s melting point (adjusted for nanoscale effects) up to the complete melting of the particle (approximately 1100–1420 °C, accounting for calibration offsets as in prior studies), followed by controlled slow cooling.
generation.structural_mediator: A transient, copper-rich liquid layer forming at the nanoparticle surface that induces local lattice strain and increases atomic diffusivity.
generation.mechanism: Due to its relatively low melting temperature, copper segregates to the nanoparticle surface and premelts, forming a liquid layer that lowers local energy barriers. This layer enhances the diffusion of the other metal atoms (Fe, Ni, Cr, Co) thereby promoting a more homogeneous melting and subsequent solid solution upon cooling. Essentially, the copper-driven surface premelting triggers a kinetic pathway that governs the overall thermal response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles will first exhibit localized surface modifications (e.g., spreading or shape changes) corresponding to copper premelting, followed by rapid homogenization as the liquid layer facilitates mixing of the remaining elements. This behavior will result in a lower effective melting onset and improved consolidation into a uniform single-phase upon cooling compared to particles without such copper segregation.
generation.baseline: A scenario where melting initiates uniformly across the particle without preferential surface phenomena, leading to a melting temperature predicted solely by the bulk thermodynamics of an ideal solid solution.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for nanoparticles below ~100 nm in diameter (where surface energy effects are dominant) and for equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions containing at least one element with a significantly lower melting point (copper); for larger particles or markedly non-equiatomic mixtures, the mechanism may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The exact interplay between copper diffusion kinetics and the local compositional fluctuations is not fully characterized. This hypothesis combines evidence from in situ neutron imaging of Cu-rich phase behavior in similar alloy systems (PMC8320920::web::011::3_results) and the observed diverse alloying kinetics in bimetallic systems (PMC10144805::web::016::3_3_mechanical_alloying_behavior_of_heap). Direct extension to the five-element HEA nanoparticles under premelting/melting conditions remains to be experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ heating experiments on the HEA nanoparticles using high-resolution imaging (e.g., cold neutron imaging or TEM heating holders) along with spatially resolved compositional analysis (EDX mapping) during incremental heating. Compare nanoparticles with varied copper contents to see if the onset of premelting and subsequent melting behavior scales with copper surface enrichment.
measurements: Surface morphology changes (e.g., onset of liquid-like spreading at the surface)
Elemental distribution profiles (particularly copper enrichment at surfaces) via EDX
Temperature thresholds for localized premelting and full melting via diffraction or optical methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no preferential copper segregation or liquid layer formation is observed at the nanoparticle surfaces prior to full melting, or if variations in copper content do not lead to measurable shifts in the premelting or melting temperatures and melting behavior, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. Mechanical Alloying Behavior of HEAPs
cited_evidence.text: The phase formation mechanism of HEAPs is mainly related to the alloying behavior of components during mechanical alloying. Due to the small difference in physical properties and electronegativity of elements in the CoCrCuFeMnNix HEA system, the alloying process is mainly diffusion-controlled. The diffusion rates of alloying elements are different due to their physical properties. Chen et al. [] showed that elements with a low melting point or brittle crystal structure may be preferentially dissolved during ball milling. Figure 9 shows the melting point and thermal conductivity of each element in the CoCrCuFeMnNi HEA system []. The melting points of Co and Ni are very similar, but Ni with an FCC phase has higher plasticity than Co with an HCP phase, so the alloying of Co occurs before Ni. Therefore, the alloying sequence of CoCrCuFeMnNix HEAPs during ball milling is Cu→Mn→Co→Ni→Fe→Cr. Generally, the solid solubility of an alloy is mainly affected by the following three factors: (1) crystal structure, (2) the atomic size of the constituent elements (i.e., the atomic size difference), (3) chemical compatibility between constituent elements (i.e., electronegativity difference or ΔHmix
